title: Angles, Parallel Lines, and Angle Relationships

objective.objectiveLatex: Identify and classify angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal, vertical angles, complementary and supplementary pairs, and apply the triangle angle sum and polygon angle sum theorems to find unknown angle measures.

prerequisites.noteLatex: Familiarity with basic angle notation and triangle interior angles from prior modules is assumed.

concept.conceptLatex:
When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, eight angles are formed with predictable relationships. Vertical angles share a vertex and have no intervening segments; they are always congruent. A linear pair of adjacent angles sums to 180, making them supplementary. Complementary angles sum to 90. If parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are congruent, alternate interior angles are congruent, alternate exterior angles are congruent, and consecutive interior angles are supplementary. These rules are reversible: if a pair of angles is congruent (or supplementary) and the lines are cut by a transversal, the lines are parallel. The triangle angle sum theorem states that the interior angles of any triangle total 180. Generalizing to a convex n-gon, the interior angle sum is (n-2) * 180 and each exterior angle, one at each vertex, sums to 360.

angle A and angle B are vertical, so angle A = angle B

angle A and angle B form a linear pair, so angle A + angle B = 180

If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then corresponding angles are congruent.

If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, then alternate interior angles are congruent.

The interior angle sum of a triangle is 180.

The interior angle sum of a convex n-gon is (n-2) * 180

items.name: Vertical angles are congruent
items.bodyLatex: \text{When two lines intersect, the opposite (vertical) angles have the same measure.}

items.name: Linear pair angles are supplementary
items.summaryLatex: \text{Angles in a linear pair sum to } 180^{\circ}	ext{.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{If two adjacent angles form a straight line, their measures add to } 180^{\circ}	ext{.}

items.name: Corresponding angles are congruent
items.summaryLatex: \text{Corresponding angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are congruent.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, angles in the same relative position are congruent.}

items.name: Alternate interior angles are congruent
items.summaryLatex: \text{Alternate interior angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are congruent.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, interior angles on opposite sides of the transversal are congruent.}

items.name: Alternate exterior angles are congruent
items.summaryLatex: \text{Alternate exterior angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are congruent.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, exterior angles on opposite sides of the transversal are congruent.}

items.name: Consecutive interior angles are supplementary
items.summaryLatex: \text{Consecutive interior angles formed by a transversal and parallel lines are supplementary.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, interior angles on the same side of the transversal sum to } 180^{\circ}	ext{.}

items.name: Triangle angle sum is 180
items.summaryLatex: \text{The interior angles of a triangle sum to } 180^{\circ}	ext{.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{For any triangle } \triangle ABC, \angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^{\circ}	ext{.}

items.name: Polygon interior angle sum
items.summaryLatex: \text{The interior angle sum of a convex } n	ext{-gon is } (n-2)\times 180^{\circ}	ext{.}
items.bodyLatex: \text{A convex } n	ext{-gon can be decomposed into } (n-2) \text{ triangles, each contributing } 180^{\circ}	ext{.}

items.titleLatex: Confusing vertical angles with adjacent angles
items.wrongLatex: \angle A = \angle B \text{ because they look the same size but share a ray}
items.whyLatex: \text{Vertical angles must be opposite each other at an intersection; adjacent angles share a ray and their sum is not guaranteed to be equal.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Look for the shared vertex and no intersecting segments between the angles. If they share a ray, they are adjacent, not vertical.}

items.wrongLatex: \angle 1 and \angle 2 are corresponding because they are both on the same side
items.whyLatex: \text{Corresponding angles must be in the same relative position at each intersection. Being on the same side alone is not sufficient.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Match the position at one intersection to the same position at the other intersection (top-left with top-left, bottom-right with bottom-right, etc.).}

items.titleLatex: Forgetting to use triangle angle sum in the correct orientation
items.wrongLatex: \angle x = 180^{\circ} - (\angle A + \angle B) \text{ when the triangle is not oriented with a base}
items.whyLatex: \text{The triangle angle sum theorem applies to interior angles regardless of orientation, but one must correctly identify which three angles belong to the triangle.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Identify the three interior angles of the triangle explicitly before applying the theorem.}
